Task 5: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

DataX Labs – Data Analyst Internship

Dataset: E-commerce Customer & Transaction Data (synthetic, 1000 records)

Objective: Extract insights using visual and statistical exploration.

Tools: Python (Pandas, Matplotlib, Seaborn)

In [1]:

Observation: The dataset has 1000 rows and 12 columns. AnnualIncome and Rating each have ~2% missing values (20 rows), which is small enough to impute with the median rather than drop. Categorical columns (Gender, City, ProductCategory) are clean with no missing values. Electronics and Fashion are the two most purchased categories.

2. Data Cleaning (light touch, for visualization purposes)¶

In [7]:
df_clean = df.copy()
df_clean['AnnualIncome'] = df_clean['AnnualIncome'].fillna(df_clean['AnnualIncome'].median())
df_clean['Rating'] = df_clean['Rating'].fillna(df_clean['Rating'].median())
print("Remaining missing values:", df_clean.isna().sum().sum())

Remaining missing values: 0

3. Univariate Analysis — Histograms¶

In [8]:
num_cols = ['Age', 'AnnualIncome', 'SpendingScore', 'Price', 'Quantity', 'Rating', 'TotalSpend']

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(16, 12))
axes = axes.flatten()
for i, col in enumerate(num_cols):
    sns.histplot(df_clean[col], kde=True, ax=axes[i], color='#4C72B0')
    axes[i].set_title(f'Distribution of {col}')
for j in range(len(num_cols), len(axes)):
    fig.delaxes(axes[j])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('../images/histograms.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Observations:

  • Age is roughly normally distributed, centered around 33–38 years.
  • AnnualIncome and Price are strongly right-skewed — a small number of high-value customers/products pull the tail out (matches the outliers we injected).
  • SpendingScore and Rating are approximately normal/symmetric.
  • Quantity is discrete and right-skewed (Poisson-like), most orders are 1–4 items.
  • TotalSpend inherits the right skew from Price.

4. Univariate Analysis — Boxplots (outlier detection)¶

In [9]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(16, 8))
axes = axes.flatten()
box_cols = ['Age', 'AnnualIncome', 'SpendingScore', 'Price', 'Rating', 'TotalSpend']
for i, col in enumerate(box_cols):
    sns.boxplot(y=df_clean[col], ax=axes[i], color='#DD8452')
    axes[i].set_title(f'Boxplot of {col}')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('../images/boxplots.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Observations: AnnualIncome and Price (and consequently TotalSpend) show clear outliers above the upper whisker — a handful of customers with very high income and a few premium-priced orders. These should be flagged for business review rather than deleted outright, since they may represent genuine high-value customers.

5. Categorical Analysis — Value Counts as Bar Charts¶

In [10]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))
df_clean['ProductCategory'].value_counts().plot(kind='bar', ax=axes[0], color='#55A868')
axes[0].set_title('Orders by Product Category')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Count')

df_clean['City'].value_counts().plot(kind='bar', ax=axes[1], color='#C44E52')
axes[1].set_title('Orders by City')

df_clean['Gender'].value_counts().plot(kind='bar', ax=axes[2], color='#8172B2')
axes[2].set_title('Orders by Gender')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('../images/categorical_counts.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Observation: Electronics and Fashion drive the highest order volumes. Gwalior leads city-wise order share (consistent with the sampling weights used), and the gender split is nearly balanced (52% Male / 48% Female).

6. Bivariate Analysis — Scatterplots¶

In [11]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))
sns.scatterplot(data=df_clean, x='Age', y='SpendingScore', hue='Gender', ax=axes[0], alpha=0.6)
axes[0].set_title('Age vs Spending Score')

sns.scatterplot(data=df_clean, x='AnnualIncome', y='SpendingScore', ax=axes[1], alpha=0.6, color='#4C72B0')
axes[1].set_title('Annual Income vs Spending Score')

sns.scatterplot(data=df_clean, x='Price', y='Quantity', ax=axes[2], alpha=0.6, color='#DD8452')
axes[2].set_title('Price vs Quantity Purchased')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('../images/scatterplots.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Observations:

  • AnnualIncome vs SpendingScore shows a mild negative trend — higher earners in this sample don't necessarily spend a higher score, consistent with the synthetic relationship.
  • Age vs SpendingScore shows no strong linear pattern, spread fairly evenly across ages for both genders.
  • Price vs Quantity shows no strong relationship — customers buy similar quantities regardless of price point, i.e. quantity is driven by need, not affordability.

7. Multivariate Analysis — Pairplot¶

In [12]:
pair_cols = ['Age', 'AnnualIncome', 'SpendingScore', 'TotalSpend']
g = sns.pairplot(df_clean[pair_cols + ['Gender']], hue='Gender', diag_kind='kde', corner=True, plot_kws={'alpha':0.5})
g.fig.suptitle('Pairwise Relationships (colored by Gender)', y=1.02)
g.savefig('../images/pairplot.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Observation: No strong pairwise linear relationships stand out visually between Age, AnnualIncome, SpendingScore, and TotalSpend — confirming these are largely independent behavioral signals in this dataset, useful for later segmentation (e.g. clustering on Income + SpendingScore).

8. Correlation Analysis — Heatmap¶

In [13]:
corr_cols = ['Age', 'AnnualIncome', 'SpendingScore', 'Price', 'Quantity', 'Rating', 'TotalSpend', 'DaysSinceLastPurchase']
corr = df_clean[corr_cols].corr()

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 7))
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='coolwarm', center=0, linewidths=0.5)
plt.title('Correlation Heatmap of Numeric Features')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('../images/heatmap.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Observations:

  • TotalSpend correlates strongly and positively with Price (r ≈ 0.67) and moderately with Quantity (r ≈ 0.31) — expected, since TotalSpend = Price x Quantity.
  • AnnualIncome shows a moderate negative correlation with SpendingScore (r ≈ -0.50), matching the pattern seeded in the data — the highest earners are not the highest spenders by score in this dataset.
  • Age, Rating, and DaysSinceLastPurchase show near-zero correlation (|r| < 0.05) with the other variables — little linear multicollinearity risk if these were used together as features in a model.

9. Category-wise Deep Dive — Boxplot of Spend by Category¶

In [14]:
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
order = df_clean.groupby('ProductCategory')['TotalSpend'].median().sort_values(ascending=False).index
sns.boxplot(data=df_clean, x='ProductCategory', y='TotalSpend', order=order, palette='viridis')
plt.xticks(rotation=30)
plt.title('Total Spend Distribution by Product Category')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('../images/spend_by_category.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Observation: Electronics has both the highest median spend and the widest spread (including the top outliers), which makes sense given higher unit prices. Books and Grocery cluster at the low end with tight, consistent spend.

10. Summary of Findings¶

  1. Data quality: ~1000 records, only ~2% missing in AnnualIncome and Rating (imputed with median); categorical fields are complete and clean.
  2. Distributions: Age, SpendingScore, and Rating are roughly symmetric. AnnualIncome, Price, and TotalSpend are right-skewed with a small set of high-value outliers worth business review (possible VIP customers / premium orders).
  3. Category trends: Electronics and Fashion dominate order volume; Electronics drives the highest revenue per order.
  4. Relationships: AnnualIncome and SpendingScore show a mild negative relationship. Most other numeric features are weakly correlated, i.e. low multicollinearity risk.
  5. Geography: Gwalior contributes the largest share of orders in this sample, followed by Delhi and Mumbai.
  6. Actionable insight: Because spending behavior isn't purely income-driven, segmentation should combine SpendingScore, ProductCategory affinity, and DaysSinceLastPurchase (recency) rather than income alone — a good next step would be an RFM-style or K-Means segmentation using these features.
